prompt: A cliff shows flat rock layers broken along a slanted crack. Every layer on one side of the crack sits 2 m lower than the matching layer on the other side. What is this feature called?
explanation: A fault is a break in rock where the rock on one side has moved past the rock on the other side. The matching layers are offset 2 m along the crack, so this is a fault.

distractor_rationales.fault: misconception: any drop in layers is a fold; a syncline bends layers down without breaking them, but these layers are broken and moved
distractor_rationales.misconception: students think layers that sit lower on one side have been folded downward

distractor_rationales.fault: misconception: any crack cutting through layers is an intrusion; an intrusion is rock that pushed in as magma, not a break where layers slid
distractor_rationales.misconception: students think any line that cuts across rock layers must be magma that pushed in

distractor_rationales.fault: misconception: any break in layers is an unconformity; an unconformity is a gap in time between layers, not a crack that offsets them
distractor_rationales.misconception: students think every break or gap seen in a set of layers is an unconformity

real_world_check: A fault is a fracture along which rock layers have moved relative to each other, offsetting matching layers.
key_category: a feature seen in rock layers

prompt: The Arctic is warming faster than most of Earth. As more sea ice melts each summer, more dark ocean water lies open to the Sun. Which statement best explains why this speeds up the warming?
choices: Melting ice releases heat that warms the nearby air and water.
Open water lets heat from deep inside Earth escape into the air.
Dark open water absorbs more sunlight than white ice does.
The thin ozone layer lets more of the Sun's heat reach the Arctic.
correct_answer: Dark open water absorbs more sunlight than white ice does.
explanation: White ice reflects most sunlight back to space. Dark open water absorbs most of it, so the ocean warms, which melts more ice and opens still more dark water.

distractor_rationales.choice: Melting ice releases heat that warms the nearby air and water.
distractor_rationales.fault: misconception: melting gives off heat; melting ice takes in heat from its surroundings
distractor_rationales.misconception: students think ice gives off heat as it melts, so melting warms the air

distractor_rationales.choice: Open water lets heat from deep inside Earth escape into the air.
distractor_rationales.fault: misconception: heat from Earth's interior drives surface warming; that heat is tiny and steady and did not change as the ice melted
distractor_rationales.misconception: students think global warming comes from heat rising out of Earth's hot interior

distractor_rationales.choice: The thin ozone layer lets more of the Sun's heat reach the Arctic.
distractor_rationales.fault: misconception: the ozone hole causes global warming; ozone loss lets in more ultraviolet light, not the extra heat behind Arctic warming
distractor_rationales.misconception: students think the hole in the ozone layer is what lets in the heat that warms the planet

real_world_check: Sea ice reflects most sunlight while open ocean absorbs most of it, so losing ice increases warming (ice-albedo feedback).
key_category: a cause of extra warming in the Arctic

prompt: A dry city on the coast has little fresh water. It builds a plant that takes the dissolved salt out of ocean water so people can drink it. What is this process called?
explanation: Taking dissolved salt out of seawater to make fresh water is called desalination. Filters, chlorine and bubbling air treat water in other ways but leave the salt in it.

distractor_rationales.fault: misconception: bubbling air through water removes what is dissolved in it; aeration adds oxygen and removes some gases, but the salt stays dissolved
distractor_rationales.misconception: students think bubbling air through water cleans everything out of it, salt included

distractor_rationales.fault: misconception: a sand filter removes salt; it catches solid bits, but dissolved salt passes straight through with the water
distractor_rationales.misconception: students think pouring salt water through sand or a filter strains the salt out

distractor_rationales.fault: misconception: adding chlorine makes seawater safe to drink; chlorine kills germs but leaves all the salt in the water
distractor_rationales.misconception: students think adding chlorine is what turns any water, even seawater, into drinking water

real_world_check: Desalination removes dissolved salts from seawater, while filtration, aeration and chlorination do not remove dissolved salt.
key_category: a process for treating water

prompt: At noon, the Moon passes in front of the Sun and hides all of it from the town of Ilvar; the sky there goes dark for two minutes. At that moment, a person in a city 3,000 km away is also on the daytime side of Earth. What will that person most likely see?
choices: A Sun that looks partly covered by the Moon, or not covered by it.
A lunar eclipse, with the Moon turning a reddish color.
The same total eclipse, with the daytime sky turning dark.
The Sun hidden behind the shadow of Earth instead of the Moon.
correct_answer: A Sun that looks partly covered by the Moon, or not covered by it.
explanation: The Moon is much smaller than Earth, so its full shadow covers only a narrow path, about 100-200 km wide. A person 3,000 km away is outside it and sees at most part of the Sun covered.

distractor_rationales.choice: A lunar eclipse, with the Moon turning a reddish color.
distractor_rationales.fault: misconception: a solar and a lunar eclipse are the same event; a lunar eclipse happens at full moon, when the Moon is on the night side, not at a solar eclipse
distractor_rationales.misconception: students mix up solar and lunar eclipses and think both happen at the same time

distractor_rationales.choice: The same total eclipse, with the daytime sky turning dark.
distractor_rationales.fault: misconception: everyone on the daytime side sees a total eclipse; the Moon's full shadow covers only a narrow path on Earth
distractor_rationales.misconception: students think a total eclipse is seen from the whole daytime side of Earth at once

distractor_rationales.choice: The Sun hidden behind the shadow of Earth instead of the Moon.
distractor_rationales.fault: misconception: a solar eclipse is caused by Earth's shadow; Earth's shadow falls on the Moon in a lunar eclipse, while the Sun is hidden only by the Moon
distractor_rationales.misconception: students think eclipses of the Sun happen when Earth's shadow covers it

real_world_check: During a solar eclipse the Moon's umbra covers a narrow path; places outside it see a partial eclipse or none.
key_category: what a viewer sees in the sky during a solar eclipse

prompt: Two igneous rocks contain the same minerals. One formed when magma hardened deep underground, and its crystals are as big as peas. The other formed when lava hardened on the surface, and its crystals are too tiny to see. Which statement best explains the difference in crystal size?
choices: The underground rock is older, and its crystals kept growing after it hardened.
The magma underground cooled slowly, giving its crystals time to grow.
Weight from rock above pressed small crystals into big ones.
Wind and rain wore the lava's large crystals down into tiny ones.
correct_answer: The magma underground cooled slowly, giving its crystals time to grow.
explanation: Magma deep underground is insulated by the rock around it, so it cools over a long time and its crystals have time to grow large. Lava on the surface cools quickly, so its crystals stay tiny.

distractor_rationales.choice: The underground rock is older, and its crystals kept growing after it hardened.
distractor_rationales.fault: misconception: crystals in solid rock keep growing with age; growth stops once the rock is solid, and crystal size is set while it cools
distractor_rationales.misconception: students think crystals in a rock keep getting bigger the older the rock is

distractor_rationales.choice: Weight from rock above pressed small crystals into big ones.
distractor_rationales.fault: misconception: pressure fuses small crystals into large ones; crystal size comes from how long crystals have to grow as the melt cools
distractor_rationales.misconception: students think squeezing makes small grains join into bigger crystals

distractor_rationales.choice: Wind and rain wore the lava's large crystals down into tiny ones.
distractor_rationales.fault: misconception: weathering makes the fine grains; the fine crystals formed when the lava cooled fast, before any weathering
distractor_rationales.misconception: students think small grains in a rock always come from the rock being worn down

real_world_check: In igneous rock, slow cooling produces large crystals and fast cooling produces small crystals.
key_category: a cause of crystal size in igneous rock

prompt: Along one coast, the plate under the ocean floor is sliding beneath the edge of a continent by about 5 cm each year. Suppose this keeps going for millions of years. Which prediction is best?
choices: Volcanoes and earthquakes will keep forming along the edge of the continent.
The edge of the continent will slowly sink under the ocean with the plate.
The ocean will dry up as its floor slides away under the land.
The two plates will lock together, and the shaking there will stop.
correct_answer: Volcanoes and earthquakes will keep forming along the edge of the continent.
explanation: Where an ocean plate slides beneath a continent, the sinking plate sticks and slips, causing earthquakes, and rock above it melts to feed volcanoes. As long as the sliding continues, both keep forming along that edge.

distractor_rationales.choice: The edge of the continent will slowly sink under the ocean with the plate.
distractor_rationales.fault: misconception: the continent goes down with the ocean plate; continental rock is too light to sink, so it rides over the denser ocean plate
distractor_rationales.misconception: students think that when two plates meet, the one being pushed on sinks under the sea

distractor_rationales.choice: The ocean will dry up as its floor slides away under the land.
distractor_rationales.fault: misconception: the sea water leaves with the sinking floor; new ocean floor forms elsewhere, and the water stays in the ocean basin
distractor_rationales.misconception: students think the ocean water goes wherever the ocean floor goes

distractor_rationales.choice: The two plates will lock together, and the shaking there will stop.
distractor_rationales.fault: misconception: plate motion stops once plates meet; the plate keeps sliding, and the sticking and slipping is what makes earthquakes
distractor_rationales.misconception: students think that once two plates touch, they stop moving and the ground becomes still

real_world_check: At ocean-continent subduction zones, the denser oceanic plate sinks beneath the continent, producing a belt of earthquakes and volcanoes along the continental edge.
key_category: a prediction of what happens where one plate slides under another
